title: AVATAR MVT interview_GENTRY BARNETT
description: Interview with Gentry Barnett Chief Technology Officer, Space Tango. The Mission Verification Test (MVT) for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) payload, marking a critical milestone ahead of the Artemis II launch. This test validated system performance as designed to confirm mission readiness.    The MVT demonstrated end-to-end functionality of the automated payload, including environmental control, power systems, data handling, and operational sequencing. By verifying performance ahead of flight, the team aims to reduce mission risk and validate ST’s automation approach, built on the heritage of hundreds of investigations previously flown on the International Space Station.
via: the NASA Image and Video Library

transcript.text: - My name is Gentry Barnett
and I am the program manager for this avatar project.
So Space Tango is proud to serve as the payload developer
for the avatar payload on the Artemis two mission.
At, at high level, the avatar payload consists
of two main pieces, the organ chip science,
and then the hardware itself.
And the hardware enables that science at a high level.
The hardware creates
and maintains an environment that's suitable
for the spine science.
Throughout the course of the mission specifically,
we provide a 37 C incubator conditions
for temperature, a humidity, a high humidity,
and 5% CO2 environment,
and a low flow rate that provides nutrients
to the organ chips.
The payload is fully automated from,
from when we turn it over at about L minus 24 hours out at
the pad until we receive it back at the port at San Diego.
The only interaction that the crew will have
with the payload is a daily button press,
which provides back telemetry to us on the ground.
That gives us a real time insight into the health
and the status of the payload norm.
The chip installation is,
is very critical is it's really the first time
that the engineering and the science teams come together.
So each of the four chips will be installed
and we have to ensure that media is consistently flowing so
that we don't introduce bubbles into those chips.
As soon as the chips are installed, we purge
that humidity surrounding the chips
with a high humidity 5% CO2 environment,
and then we immediately need to get those up to
that 37 c incubation temperature.
All these steps are really time critical
and they have inherent risk associated with them
that could impact the mission.
And so that's really why the chip installation process is
probably the most critical in our late load operations.
We've overcome several engineering challenges
with sending live tissue into space
with this avatar payload.
The exterior structure itself was very unique in
that we had a, a very specific spot within the Orion
vehicle, and that's what led to the,
the interesting trapezoid shape of the unit itself.
So inside that exterior structure are two additional
structures, and those provide the levels of containment
that keep the crew safe from the biology within,
but also keeps that biology safe from the vibration
and shock effects from launch and return.
Other than structure, power has been really a,
a unique challenge to overcome.
So the avatar payload itself provides its own power.
So we had to create our own custom power system
that included lithium batteries
and protection subsystems
that meet all the NASA requirements.
This provided only enough power
to support our thermal subsystem,
and so on top of that, we,
we designed our own fluidic system
that is a powerless system that provides
that low constant media exchange
throughout the course of the mission.
So we designed a, a kind of a nested foam design
with the organoid chips in the center of that and,
and that protects those chips from the vibration
and shock effects of the launch and return loadings.
And we've been through several tests, NASA safety
and verification tests
that have validated these designs throughout the, our,
our years of development for flight, we're going to,
to develop and, and, and put together two pairs of units.
And so for each pair, that will be one flight
and one ground unit.
And this allows the PI team to use that science data
after the mission is over to really isolate the effects of,
of microgravity in the space flight environment versus those
effects that are coming from the avatar payload itself.
So when this payload finally gets installed into Orion,
you know, I will be filled with great pride really
for this team, that it's, it represents
this team is filled with highly skilled engineers
and scientists that are enabling this,
this groundbreaking science
to happen on such an historic mission for America's return
to the moon avatar really enables us to learn about
how humans react in a space flight environment, you know,
especially on, on the lunar surface.
And even when we go beyond that.
So from Moon to Mars, we've gotta learn
and we've gotta know before we go.
And so this type of technology allows us
to have these answers before we send our our Americans.
Yeah, this week we're preparing for launch, so we run
through all of our last minute loading
and operational procedures to ensure that all
of our verification requirements
and safety requirements are marked off.
Then we will take the, the payload out to the pad,
perform our last minute checkoffs there,
and hand that over to be installed on Orion.
